The fact matters for the research question because Patrick's place of birth bears on the family's geographic and national origin, and on whether the Thomas Flynn household is his family of origin.

The 1860 federal census (src_003, a_009) records Patrick at age 15, born Ireland, in the same household. Both are original government schedules; the household informant for birthplace in both cases was almost certainly Thomas Flynn or his wife — Patrick's parents, who witnessed and directly knew where their child was born. The 1908 death certificate (src_004, a_012) records birthplace as Pennsylvania; informant was James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law, who supplied personal details about the deceased. Brown was not present at Patrick's birth circa 1845 and could have known his father-in-law's birthplace only by report.

The census records are more reliable for this fact. Patrick's parents are the strongest possible informants for a child's birthplace — they were present, they carried that knowledge forward, and they reported it consistently to two different enumerators a decade apart. James Brown, by contrast, had no firsthand knowledge. He knew Patrick as a Pennsylvania man; Ireland was a chapter of Patrick's life that preceded Brown's acquaintance with him entirely.

The death certificate's 'Pennsylvania' reflects the immigration origin confusion pattern: after roughly 60 years of Pennsylvania residence, Patrick's American home had become the family's sole lived reality. A son-in-law who met Patrick only in that context — who never knew him as an immigrant, never heard stories that foregrounded an Irish birth — would naturally associate 'where Patrick was from' with Pennsylvania. This is a well-documented error class in records produced by American-born or American-assimilated informants reporting on immigrant ancestors: the family's long-established American home displaces the foreign birthplace from working memory. The error is not random; it names precisely the state where Patrick had lived for his entire American life, pointing to the specific epistemic gap of an informant who knew the deceased only in one country.
